title: The Cause of Much Pain
preamble: In 22 clues, one letter has somehow moved to the clue above. These letters must be returned to the correct clues before solving, always creating or leaving behind real words. In clue order the letters spell out a phrase which indicates how five thematically relevant answers must be moved in the completed grid, letters displaced from other answers moving to fill gaps so created and always keeping their original order. A sixth movement is required, but it does not reach the level of the others and in doing so re-enacts a supposed historical event; solvers must highlight the principle involved. Chambers Dictionary (2003) is the primary reference.

messages.text: WHAT GOES UP MUST COME DOWN

clue.text: Smitten sweep travelling west carrying nurse's heart

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other
across clues read left to right, so heading west runs the letters the other way

parts.note: printed with a W that belongs to the clue below; restored it reads seep, for which sipe is a Chambers synonym

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of nurse

explanation.surface: A lovesick chimney sweep heading west with a nurse on his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: The W in 'sweep' is the moved letter, starting the phrase WHAT GOES UP MUST COME DOWN. Restored, seep gives SIPE, which turns round to EPIS and takes in R.
explanation.definitionFit: Épris is a French borrowing listed by Chambers meaning enamoured, the lovestruck state of a person who has fallen for someone.

clue.text: Breaking secondary picket could present red Tony with means of reducing selling

definitions.note: printed 'selling' is 'swelling' with its W moved up to the clue above, as the preamble says

indicators.note: breaking the words apart signals that the letters of secondary picket are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder: its fifteen letters hold the answer's eight plus those of red Tony
the letters left over once the answer is taken out of the fodder

explanation.surface: A trade-union dispute: a secondary picket could hand a left-wing Tony something to cut sales.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, this clue's W has moved to 1 across (turning 'seep' into 'sweep'); restored, the definition reads 'means of reducing swelling'. Rearranging SECONDARYPICKET gives the answer plus the letters of RED TONY.
explanation.definitionFit: Packs of ice are pressed on a sprain or bruise to bring inflammation down, so they reduce swelling.

clue.text: Plausible lines added to copy of will, expunging the rights of Auntie Ruth

indicators.note: added to puts the lines on after what is left of the copy of the will
expunging means striking out, so letters are taken out of the copy of the will

parts.note: probate is the official copy of a proven will
the rights are the right-hand, final letters: E of Auntie and T of Rut, Ruth's H having slipped up from the clue below

explanation.surface: A will has been doctored, Auntie Ruth's claims struck out, and the new wording sounds plausible enough.
explanation.walkthrough: A letter has strayed here: the H of Ruth belongs to 12-across, so read Auntie Rut, and 'the rights of' takes the last letter of each. 'Expunging' removes them from PROBATE to leave PROBA, and 'added to' puts the lines after.
explanation.definitionFit: Proball is a Shakespearean word, listed in Chambers, meaning probable or credible, so it is a fair synonym of plausible.

clue.text: Equip in full all but eight (6, two words)

indicators.note: all but means everything except, so some letters are left out

parts.note: right out means completely, to the full extent
printed without its H, which has gone up to 10 across; restored it is height, abbreviated HT

explanation.surface: Kitting out a whole rowing crew bar one boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eight' looks like the rowing crew, but restoring its lost H makes height, and HT is its standard abbreviation, removed from RIGHT OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To rig someone out is to fit them up with clothes or gear, the usual phrasal verb for equipping fully.

clue.text: Tip fag end on sheet

parts.note: Chambers gives lag as the hindmost part, the fag end
a nappe is a sheet, of rock in geology or of water falling over a weir

explanation.surface: Flicking a cigarette butt onto a bedsheet, or an ashtray instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' tempts as a verb for dropping the fag end; it is the noun meaning a gratuity. A fag is British slang for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A lagniappe, from Louisiana French, is a small bonus or gratuity given to a customer, much as a tip is a small extra given.

clue.text: Ahead of noon and king's to be found in beer joint

indicators.note: what is found in something sits inside it, so these letters are placed within another

parts.note: ale is a type of beer

indicators.note: printed with an extra letter; restored as head it points at the leading letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the first letter of noon
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A king drinking in a pub before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: The A in 'Ahead' belongs to 17 across's 'lunch', making launch; with it gone the clue reads head of noon. 'Beer joint' looks like a pub, but joint is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ankle is the hinge where the foot meets the leg, one of the body's best-known articulations.

clue.text: One interrupting interminable complimentary lunch

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into, so one piece sits in the middle of another
something interminable has no end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: complimentary means given free of charge
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone butting in during a never-ending free lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunch' has lost its A to 15 across's 'Ahead'; restored it reads launch, so the free meal is a decoy and the definition is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire a rocket or missile is to launch it, sending it off into the air.

clue.text: Deft fish swallows a mound of debris

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a sar, or sargus, is a sea bream
a tell is an archaeological mound built up from the remains of settlements

explanation.surface: A nimble fish gulping down a heap of rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deft' carries the T of 21 across's 'top'; without it the definition is def, slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Def is hip-hop slang for first-rate, and stellar is the informal word for outstanding, star-quality performance.

clue.text: Stupidly narrow-minded and backward girl almost cut the op

parts.note: short for po-faced, which Chambers glosses as stupidly solemn and narrow-minded

indicators.note: going backward means reading from the far end towards the start
almost means not quite all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: Della is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A dim, bigoted girl botching the surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Op' has lost its T to 19 across's 'Deft'; restored, 'cut the top' is the definition, and the hospital operation is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Polled trees have been pollarded and polled cattle dehorned: in both cases the top has been lopped off.

clue.text: In Oz, dog bone tipped with gold

parts.note: Chambers gives tot as a bone or other item salvaged from refuse
printed with a G from the clue below; restored it reads old, abbreviated O

explanation.surface: An Australian dog's bone with a golden tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Oz' suggests Australia, but it is the Land of Oz. The G of 'gold' belongs to 23 across's 'win', making wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Toto is Dorothy's little dog in The Wizard of Oz, the companion who follows her down the yellow brick road.

clue.text: Garter-snake upset asp after win

indicators.note: after places the piece it introduces second, behind what follows it

parts.note: printed without its G, which has gone up to 22 across; restored as wing, it is el, an extension of a building

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: One snake annoyed when another snake wins.
explanation.walkthrough: With its G restored 'win' becomes wing, and an el (or ell) is a wing added to a building.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaps is a genus of small venomous snakes, and Chambers gives garter-snake as one of its common names.

clue.text: Abandoning new rule, Lord Lieutenants smashed up bangers

indicators.note: smashed up means broken into pieces, so the letters of Lord Lieutenants are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder: the letters of these two words, less those named after Abandoning
R is the Chambers abbreviation for rule

explanation.surface: Officials who ignore a fresh regulation end up demolishing a heap of sausages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoning' tells you to drop N (new) and R (rule) from the fifteen letters of LORD LIEUTENANTS; the remaining thirteen, 'smashed up', give the answer. A banger is British slang for a sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: Andouillettes are small French sausages made of chitterlings, and sausages are what British slang calls bangers.

clue.text: Moan goodbye to …

parts.note: vale is Latin for farewell
t' is the clipped dialect form, the dots marking the word cut short

explanation.surface: Grumbling a farewell, trailing off into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moan' carries the O of 32 across's 'huffs'; without it the definition is man, in the sense of a manservant.
explanation.definitionFit: A man in the old sense is a male servant, and a valet is a gentleman's personal manservant.

clue.text: … huffs, only child, roughly ten, leaving infants

definitions.note: with the O returned from 29-across this is houffs, Scots for haunts or pubs (a variant of howffs)

indicators.note: leaving means these letters depart from the word for infants

parts.note: innocents are young children, babes
OC is the Chambers abbreviation for only child
roughly signals that the letters of ten come jumbled, here as ENT

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: someone sulks, a lone child of about ten walking out on the little ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The O printed in 'Moan' at 29-across belongs here, making the definition houffs, Scots for haunts. From INNOCENTS remove OC and ENT (ten 'roughly') to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A houff or howff is a Scottish word for a regular haunt, especially a pub, so houffs are drinking places.

clue.text: Brick office bases

parts.note: a bur or burr is a mass of hard-burnt brick
a den is a private room for work or study

explanation.surface: Brick-built offices forming the foundations of a site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bases' carries the E of 36 across's 'Go'; without it the definition is bass, in the musical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A burden in music is the bass line or drone of a song or bagpipe, the low part underpinning the tune.

clue.text: Go warn, perhaps, journalist about one coming with teeth

indicators.note: about means around, so the collected letters surround one more

parts.note: printed without its E, which sits in 34 across; restored it is ego, Latin for I
vor is a Shakespearean word whose meaning Chambers gives only tentatively as warn
ED, short for editor
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A reporter told to buzz off, then showing his teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: With its E restored 'Go' becomes ego, I. 'Perhaps' belongs with warn because Chambers' meaning for vor is only a guess.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivories is slang for teeth, so something ivoried is furnished with them.

clue.text: Beat an unknown, one of the slowest in the RAF

parts.note: y is an algebraic unknown

parts.words: one of the slowest in the RAF
parts.note: printed with an S from 40 across; restored it is lowest, and an erk is an aircraftman, the bottom rank

explanation.surface: Outpacing an anonymous dawdler in the Royal Air Force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slowest' carries the S of 40 across's 'He'; restored to lowest, it points to ERK, British service slang for the most junior airman.
explanation.definitionFit: Yerk is an old dialect verb, listed in Chambers, meaning to strike or lash, so it means to beat.

clue.text: He created a colourful hero from orc zygotes

indicators.note: taken from the run of letters, so the answer is lifted out of the words that follow

parts.note: the first five letters, running across the word break

explanation.surface: A fantasy author breeding a hero from goblin embryos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' has lost its S to 38 across's 'slowest'; restored it reads She, because the creator is a woman. The colourful hero is the Scarlet Pimpernel.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroness Orczy wrote The Scarlet Pimpernel, whose hero is literally named for a red flower.

clue.text: French chalk's used at first on making love wearing support

definitions.note: French chalk is, i.e. the answer is French chalk

indicators.note: on means the first letter is put ahead of what follows
at first takes only the opening letter of the preceding word

parts.note: the U here has slipped up from 44-across; restored, the word is sed, whose first letter is taken (the second as printed)

indicators.note: wearing means one thing is worn around another, so at it goes inside the support

parts.note: a tee is the support a golf ball stands on
at it is slang for busy having sex

explanation.surface: Talc proves useful when a couple's passion is played out against some prop.
explanation.walkthrough: The U of 'used' has strayed up from 44-across, so read sed, and 'at first' takes its opening letter. 'Wearing' sets at it inside the golf support, making TEATITE, and 'on' puts the first letter in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Steatite is soapstone, a soft talc mineral, and French chalk is the name tailors give that soft talc.

clue.text: Honeydew melon, just the starter we'd sent back, having found nit left inside

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of melon

indicators.note: these go inside, so one pair is placed within the rest

parts.note: printed without its U, which has moved up to 41 across; restored as unit, it is I, the numeral one

indicators.note: sending back returns the letters the way they came

parts.note: the contraction's letters, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A diner sends back the honeydew melon starter after finding a louse egg in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honeydew melon' reads as one fruit, but the definition is honeydew alone. 'Nit' has lost a U and is really unit, which gives I.
explanation.definitionFit: Honeydew is a sticky deposit on leaves, and Chambers gives mildew as one of its senses, the blight found on plants.

clue.text: Bank's quiet without spin

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: tace is Latin for be silent, used in English as a call for quiet
printed with a P from 46 across; restored it reads sin, and to err is to sin

explanation.surface: A bank boasting of keeping quiet without any spin doctoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking but means outside. 'Spin' carries the P from 46 across's 'ale'; restored, the word is sin.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrace is a raised level bank of earth, like the flat steps cut into a hillside.

clue.text: Welsh girl swallowing all but the last drop of ale from close to the English border?

definitions.text: from close to the English border?

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Siân is a Welsh girl's name

indicators.text: all but the last drop of
indicators.note: everything except the final drop means the last letter is lost

parts.note: printed without its P, which sits in 45 across; restored it is pale, and lurid can mean ghastly pale

explanation.surface: A Welsh girl downing a pint of ale near the border with England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ale' has lost its P; restored it is pale, which Chambers gives as one sense of lurid. The question mark flags a definition by description.
explanation.definitionFit: The Silures were an ancient tribe of south-east Wales, close to the English border, and Silurian means belonging to them.

clue.text: Played out time in old squadron

parts.note: i' is the old clipped form of in
the Royal Navy's fleet was once split into red, white and blue squadrons

explanation.surface: A worn-out veteran's time in a former air squadron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Played out' looks like a game ending but means exhausted. The Admiral of the Red commanded one of the navy's historical coloured squadrons.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone played out has no energy left, the state of being worn out or exhausted.

clue.text: Measures of hemp, hashish

indicators.note: of here means drawn out of, so only a stretch from inside the words that follow is kept and the letters around it go

parts.note: printed with an M that belongs to 2 down's trap (making tramp); with it returned, the word is hep

explanation.surface: Quantities of cannabis being weighed out.
explanation.walkthrough: The M in 'hemp' has strayed up from 2 down; once it goes back, 'hep hashish' holds the answer from the second letter onwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The ephah was a Hebrew dry measure for grain, named in the Bible, so the plural names units of volume.

clue.text: Person regularly avoided trap

indicators.note: skipping at regular intervals leaves every other letter

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of person

explanation.surface: Someone who habitually steered clear of a snare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trap' has lost its M to 1 down's 'hemp'; restored it is tramp, in the sense of a promiscuous woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Tramp is a dated slur for a promiscuous woman, and pro is slang for a prostitute.

clue.text: Duress down under finally cut short Aussie oaf having trouble without money

definitions.note: printed with a U that belongs to 4 down's sites (making suites); with it returned the definition reads dress down, a verb phrase meaning to scold

indicators.note: finally points to the end of under, so only its closing letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of under

indicators.note: cutting the oaf short docks the last letter from his word

parts.note: an ocker is Australian slang for an uncouth, boorish man

indicators.note: trouble without money is trouble with the currency taken out of it

parts.note: the rouble is the Russian unit of currency

explanation.surface: An Australian lout, broke and in trouble, gets a scolding down under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' looks like one phrase meaning Australia, but once the stray U in 'Duress' goes back to 4 down, 'Dress down' is the definition and 'under' starts the wordplay. An ocker is an Australian boor.
explanation.definitionFit: To rocket someone is British slang for giving a severe reprimand, which is exactly what a dressing-down is.

clue.text: Wood used to make sites, perhaps, in the aspect of overturned goddess

definitions.text: Wood used to make sites, perhaps

indicators.note: turned over in a down clue means read from the bottom up

parts.note: as means in the role or character of
Pele is the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes

explanation.surface: Timber chosen for building sites, laid out to honour a toppled goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sites' has lost its U to 3 down's 'Duress'; restored it is suites, sets of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapele is a West African mahogany-like hardwood, widely used for furniture such as dining or bedroom suites.

clue.text: Misfortunes? Rather not say!

indicators.note: not excludes something, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: rather! and I'll say! are both emphatic agreement
printed with an S from 6 down; restored it reads ay, yes

explanation.surface: Asked about bad luck, someone would prefer not to discuss it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rather!' is the British exclamation of keen agreement. Restoring 'say' to ay, the removal leaves I'LL S.
explanation.definitionFit: Ills are troubles or misfortunes, as in the ills of the world.

clue.text: Shifting and, after sign of hesitation, beginning to go

parts.note: er is the sound of hesitating

indicators.note: a beginning is the start, so only the first letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of go

explanation.surface: Someone fidgeting and hesitating before setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' has lost its S to 5 down's 'say'; restored the definition is shifting sand.
explanation.definitionFit: An erg is a vast area of shifting sand dunes in the Sahara.

clue.text: A number of card holders knock tout who's only just left?

parts.note: a PIN is the personal number a cardholder keys in
printed with a T from 8 down; restored it reads knock out, abbreviated KO

explanation.surface: A ticket tout getting beaten up by a crowd of punters as he barely escapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tout' carries the T of 8 down's 'urn'. 'Only just left' sounds like departing; the question mark signals the political sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinko is someone mildly socialist, pink rather than red, so only slightly to the political left.

clue.text: Get one old urn for a flier

parts.note: to cop is to get or catch
the Roman numeral for one
printed without its T, which has gone up to 7 down; restored as old turn, lot is one's allotted turn

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' looks like a printed handbill but means someone who flies. 'Urn' has lost its T and is really turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-pilot is the second pilot of an aircraft, someone who flies it alongside the captain.

clue.text: Cox nearly drowns gutless Arabs, perhaps

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the end letter is lost

parts.note: printed with a C from 11 down; restored it reads ox, and a steer is a young castrated ox

indicators.note: removing the guts leaves only the outside letters

parts.note: the outer letters of drowns

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cox' suggests a rowing cox, but its C belongs to 11 down's 'Dane'. Arabs are a famous breed of horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A steed is a horse, especially a spirited riding horse, and Arabs are one well-known example.

clue.text: Dane in Scotland, we note, is swell

parts.note: printed without its C, which sits in 9 down; restored it is dance, and a ball is a formal dance
oo is a Scots form of we

explanation.surface: A Danish visitor north of the border says everything is great.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like an adjective for splendid but is a verb. 'Dane' has lost a C and is really dance.
explanation.definitionFit: To balloon is to swell out or inflate, as a sail or a debt does.

clue.text: A universal good character

parts.note: taken as written
U is the film-rating abbreviation for universal
printed with an O from 16 down; restored it reads god, and Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: A thoroughly decent person, admired by all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good character' reads as a phrase, but 'good' carries the O of 16 down's 'try'; restored it is god.
explanation.definitionFit: An aura is the distinctive atmosphere or quality surrounding a person, close to their character.

clue.text: Something written in Java: try out fruit

indicators.note: out means removed, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: an applet is a small program, classically written in the Java language
printed without its O, which has gone up to 14 down; restored it is troy, abbreviated T

explanation.walkthrough: Java looks like the island but is the programming language. 'Try' has lost an O and is really troy, the weight system abbreviated T.
explanation.definitionFit: The apple is the classic orchard fruit, and in this puzzle the one that fell on Newton's head.

clue.text: Hydrocarbon network turning up in compound

indicators.note: in means inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: ree is a Scots word for a walled enclosure

indicators.note: turning upward in a down clue reads the letters from the bottom

parts.note: a net is a mesh, a network of knotted cords

explanation.surface: A chemical web appearing inside a molecule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compound' looks chemical, matching 'Hydrocarbon', but it is an enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: Retene is a crystalline hydrocarbon obtained from pine tar and fossil resins.

clue.text: Mutter "no" to returning string instrument

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters run the opposite way

parts.note: taken as written
t' is the clipped dialect form
a gue is an old Shetland violin

explanation.surface: A musician grumbling a refusal before picking up the fiddle again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mutter' carries the M of 24 down's 'For'; without it the definition is utter.

clue.text: For a link with missing leaders of Icelandic sledge expedition, arrest missing British climber

parts.note: printed without its M, which sits in 20 down; restored as form a link, it is liaise

indicators.note: leaders are at the front, so first letters are picked out

parts.note: the first letters of the three words

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step

parts.note: to nab is to arrest

explanation.definitionFit: A liana is a woody climbing plant of tropical forests, the kind that hangs from trees.

clue.text: Troublemaker's the first to spray stripe on casualty in Boston

parts.note: the first letter of spray

in the US, the hospital casualty department is the ER

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripe' carries the E of 27 down's 'Dad'. Casualty is the British name for an emergency department.

clue.text: Dad capturing two rooks with a bit of ease for famous naturalist

indicators.note: to capture is to hold inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: printed without its E, which sits in 25 down; restored it is dead, and dull means lifeless

parts.note: the first letter of ease

clue.text: To endure mobile service, more than one gorged

explanation.definitionFit: An abysm is an old poetic word for an abyss, a deep chasm, and gorges are deep narrow valleys.

clue.text: Independent newspaper supporting a pound off?

clue.text: Overly artificial, a producer of food hoard for koalas to chew?

the first three letters of artificial, its standard dictionary abbreviation

parts.note: in animal breeding, to nick is to mate successfully
printed without its O, which sits in 31 down; restored it is anon, short for anonymous, A

clue.text: Some seized in arrest were supplying barbiturate, maybe

indicators.note: only some of arrest is wanted, its closing stretch, so the opening letters are dropped
seized in points to the word grabbed by the end of that stretch, of which only the opening is caught, so its last letter goes
